description: We are a team from Pouso Alegre, Brazil, with backgrounds in civil engineering, business administration and mobile game development. We enjoy solving real problems with creativity and practical tools, and we want to build something useful and fun with NASA data. Everyone is welcome, including beginners! We are looking for people with skills in coding, data analysis, graphic design, animation and storytelling.
summary:
Mission Forge is a browser game where 1 to 4 players design a Moon lander and fly it through a complete mission. Players fill 8 slots (rocket, frame, dust covers, power, insulation, antenna, radiation shield and instruments) while balancing three real limits: budget, mass and energy. The mission then plays out in six stages: launch, a solar storm, landing among boulders, abrasive dust, a lunar day of science and a 14-day night at −130 °C. When something fails, the game explains why with real science and suggests a fix, so players learn by redesigning and flying again.
At its core is materials science: aluminum, aluminum-lithium, titanium and carbon fiber have real densities and thermal expansion, and no material wins everywhere. Four missions (south pole, far side, a shadowed crater and a two-night stay) change the rules, so the best lander changes too. Team mode gives four roles on one device, and design codes let players share and compare.
It matters because it turns real engineering trade-offs, backed by NASA data, into decisions anyone can make and understand in minutes.
details:
What it does
Mission Forge is a browser game where 1 to 4 players design a lunar lander and fly it through a full mission. Players choose a rocket, frame material, dust covers, power, insulation, antenna, radiation shield and instruments, while keeping three real limits in balance: budget, mass and energy. The mission then runs through six stages: launch, a solar storm, landing among boulders, abrasive dust, a lunar day of science and a 14-day night at −130 °C. Two decisions during flight belong to the player. At the end, a report gives up to three stars and explains every failure with real science and a suggested fix.

How it is creative
The core is materials science. Aluminum, aluminum-lithium, titanium and carbon fiber have real densities and thermal expansion, and no material wins everywhere: a frame that is light may crack on a hard landing or after a freezing night. Four missions change the rules (south pole, far side with a relay satellite, a permanently shadowed crater, and a two-night stay), so the best lander is different each time. A friendly robot mascot guides new players, and team mode gives four roles on one device.

Benefits and impact
Students learn engineering trade-offs by failing, understanding why and trying again, in minutes and without installing anything. It works on computers, tablets and phones, in English and Portuguese, and is designed for classrooms.

Tools
HTML5, JavaScript and Canvas for the pixel art, with no frameworks; a single file that runs offline. We tested game balance by simulating every possible lander design. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help with code and text.

What we considered
Scientific accuracy (every fact is sourced), simplicity for beginners, accessibility on mobile, and fair balance so that no single design wins every mission.
